# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# A careful reading of Varga and Holm's re-examination of the Halden pilot

**Bottom line:** The forensic sections (1 to 5) are valuable. They use the microdata to confirm, and put numbers on, the main suspected weaknesses of the Halden pilot. The conclusion is a different matter. The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" goes well beyond the comment's own estimates, rests on a thin novelty argument, and leaves out the one piece of randomised evidence that cuts against it.

## 1. The arithmetic: mostly right, with one inconsistency and one misstatement

**These figures check out:**
- 95.1 / 0.8 → +18.9%
- 98.4 / 0.859 → +14.6% (34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, a 14.1% fall)
- 95.4 / 0.861 → +10.8% (34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, a 13.9% fall)
- Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 → −2.6%
- The hours reduction is overstated by 20 − 14.1 ≈ 6 points.

**The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** Four scheduled 8-hour days plus 0.7 extra hours a day plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives:

32 + 2.8 + 1.6 = **36.4 hours**, not the reported 34.6.

Either the components or the total is wrong, possibly a transposition of 36.4. This matters. If actual hours were 36.4, the fall would be only about 10%, and the per-hour gain smaller still (about +9% on manager output). The authors should reconcile this.

**The abstract overstates what was corrected.** It says that "correcting the first three" problems (attrition, output measure and hours) brings the gain down to 10.8%. Table 2 corrects only **output and hours**. Attrition is described but never adjusted for. The 10.8% is still an estimate on survivors.

**The novelty extrapolation is slightly off.** A straight line through 0.61 at month 3 and 0.29 at month 6 reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not month ten. This is minor; the bigger problems with the argument are covered in section 4.

## 2. What the comment adds

- **Attrition was misreported.** The working paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The exit data show that seven withdrew after the schedule began and six cited workload or output. This is the most serious finding against the original paper. I took the original description at face value in my first review and called the withdrawals "less concerning"; that was wrong.
- **Manager ratings were inflated.** In 19 of 23 organisations, managers rated output higher than their own records showed, by 3.8 points on average.
- **Actual hours fell about 14%, not 20%.** This confirms the suspicion raised by the pilot's own fourth limitation.
- **Revenue fell in real terms**, by about 2.6%.
- **The sector claim is mechanical.** The comment makes the same point as before: any output index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain.

The data note is also honest about the main caveat: the corrected subsets were not chosen at random.

## 3. Weaknesses in the forensic sections

- **Attrition is described but not bounded.** The microdata might hold outcomes for the withdrawing organisations. Even without them, a simple bound is possible. If the nine had an output index around 85, the pooled index would drop by only about 1.5 to 2 points. That suggests attrition is a smaller bias than the other two, though still a real one.
- **No uncertainty is reported.** The 10.8% comes from 17 organisations with no confidence interval. "Less than half the reported gain" is a point comparison.
- **Small subsets are generalised.** The 3.8-point gap comes from 23 organisations, and the retail −11.2% from just **3**. The authors then talk about the output measure "overstating output by roughly four points" as if this applied to the whole pilot.
- **Selection direction is unknown.** Organisations with time tracking and submitted records are probably weighted towards professional services and IT. Whether that biases the corrected gain up or down isn't discussed.
- **The CPI deflator is rough.** Sector output prices may not have tracked consumer prices. The direction of the correction is right, but its size is uncertain.

## 4. The novelty argument is the weakest part

- **It rests on two data points.** Two observations of a self-reported energy scale can't establish a linear decay, let alone predict a zero point. Effects like this often fade quickly and then level off.
- **Energy is not output.** The comment assumes that falling energy means falling productivity but never checks. The pilot collected the output index **every month**. The obvious test is whether per-hour output declined from month 1 to month 6. The authors had the microdata and didn't report it.
- **The burden of proof works both ways.** Six months can't show the effect is durable. It equally can't show it is entirely novelty. "We cannot rule out novelty" is supported. "The gain is entirely novelty" is a separate claim that needs its own evidence.

## 5. The use of the Varden trial is selective

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature". But the same trial, using the same methods, also found:

> Case-processing offices: output per **actual** hour **+12.5% (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**. That is randomised, with record-based output and timesheet hours, at **nine months**.

That result addresses exactly the problems the comment raises:
- selection, through randomisation
- manager inflation, through administrative records
- scheduled-hours bias, through timesheets
- partly duration, at nine months, which is past the comment's own predicted zero point for energy.

It is also close to the comment's corrected 10.8%. A comment concluding that gains are "entirely an artifact" needs to deal with this result. Leaving it out while praising the trial's other stratum is a serious omission.

The comment is right that novelty could still affect Varden, since staff were unblinded. But that is a reason to wait for Varden's 24-month follow-up, not a reason to declare the effect zero now.

## 6. The meetings critique misdescribes the Varden analysis

- **It wasn't selected after the results were known.** Varden collected the meeting data in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. The data were unregistered, but that is not the same as chosen after seeing outcomes.
- **It isn't a post hoc subgroup.** Case-processing was a pre-registered randomisation stratum.
- **It argues against a claim Varden didn't make.** Varden said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test. The comment's warning that it "should not be cited as a mechanism" repeats Varden's own caveat.
- **There is supporting evidence it ignores.** In the Halden interviews, 47 of 58 managers independently described cutting meetings.
- **It works against the comment's own thesis.** If the gain comes from removing low-value meetings, it is neither a measurement artifact nor a novelty effect. It is a structural change that could well last.

The comment's statistical caution about seven offices is fair (that r = 0.71 has an interval of roughly −0.1 to 0.95). Its account of how the analysis came about is not.

## 7. Internal inconsistencies

| Where | Claim |
|---|---|
| Abstract | The four problems "account for **most** of the reported gain" |
| Abstract and conclusion | Gains are "**entirely** an artifact" |
| Data note | Corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole" |
| Conclusion | Generalises to "reduced-hours schemes" in general |

The conclusion also runs together two separate questions. One is whether output per hour rises; the evidence suggests yes, modestly. The other is whether the reduction pays for itself; in coverage-bound work it clearly doesn't. The second does not settle the first.

## 8. What the three documents together support

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Halden's 23.4% headline | Overstated, roughly by half, through manager inflation, scheduled hours and survivor bias |
| Per-hour gain in work not tied to presence | Probably real but modest, around 10–12%. Two independent sources, one randomised, roughly agree |
| Durability | Unknown. Novelty is plausible but untested; Varden's 24-month follow-up is the key evidence |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per employee falls about 10%, and service gets worse. Consistent across both datasets |
| Mechanism | Unresolved. Cutting meetings is plausible and testable; rest is asserted but untested |
| "Sector-general" (Halden) | Not supported |
| "Entirely an artifact" (Varga and Holm) | Not supported |

The comment's recommendations for future evaluations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, a comparison group, at least 18 months of follow-up, and analysis of all enrolled organisations. Its own conclusion should be held to the same standard.
